clinicalPearls: Intestinal ischemia arises when splanchnic perfusion cannot meet the metabolic demands of the gut; it is broadly divided into chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) and acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), with the latter carrying a high mortality (~50-80%) and depending critically on early diagnosis and prompt intervention (p.2586).
AMI is mechanistically categorized into three patterns: arterio-occlusive (embolic or thrombotic), nonocclusive (vasospastic/hypoperfusion), and mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587).

Roughly half of AMI cases are embolic, with emboli typically lodging in the mid-to-distal superior mesenteric artery (SMA) just beyond the origin of the middle colic artery; about 25-30% are acute-on-chronic thrombosis on preexisting mesenteric atherosclerosis (p.2586-2587).

The hallmark of acute arterial mesenteric ischemia is severe, abrupt, nonremitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical examination findings, present in roughly 95% of cases (p.2588).
Pain is disproportionate to exam because ischemia begins in the mucosal layer and advances outward toward the serosa, so peritoneal signs and cardiovascular collapse are late developments (p.2588).

CMI classically presents with insidious, recurrent dull crampy postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina'), fear of eating, and consequent weight loss, often over 6-12 months, in a malnourished patient with other signs of atherosclerosis (p.2587).

CT angiography with 1-mm or thinner cuts is the gold-standard diagnostic test for both acute and chronic mesenteric arterial occlusive disease; a venous-phase study aids detection of mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587-2588).

Fasting mesenteric duplex ultrasound is a useful screening tool: a high SMA peak flow velocity carries about an 80% positive predictive value, and a negative duplex study virtually excludes mesenteric ischemia (p.2587).

In suspected AMI the decision to operate is frequently driven by a high index of suspicion from history and exam despite normal laboratory values, and surgical consultation should not be delayed (p.2588).
Mesenteric venous thrombosis (<10% of cases) tends to be associated with hypercoagulable states; documented inherited thrombophilia warrants long-term anticoagulation (p.2587, p.2588-2589).

Severity of ischemic colonic mucosal injury is graded by colonoscopy from mild (minimal erythema) to moderate (pale ulcerations extending into muscularis) to severe (black/green discoloration indicating full-thickness necrosis) (p.2589).
harrison.pathophysiology: The intestine is perfused by the celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery (SMA), and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), with extensive collateralization through the mesenteric arcades; small-bowel collaterals converge at the duodenum and pancreatic bed, while colonic collaterals meet at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and the descending/sigmoid colon (Sudeck's point), the watershed zones most prone to colonic ischemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to ~30% of cardiac output, and protective mechanisms include abundant collaterals, autoregulation of flow, and the capacity to increase oxygen extraction. Occlusive ischemia results from embolic or thrombotic interruption of a major mesenteric artery (emboli, originating from the heart in >75% of cases, preferentially lodge in the SMA distal to the middle colic origin); development of chronic intestinal angina generally requires significant stenosis of two of the three major vessels, with SMA involvement most concerning. CMI reflects failure to mount the normal postprandial hyperemic increase in intestinal blood flow, analogous to cardiac angina, due to atherosclerotic narrowing of the SMA and/or celiac origins. Nonocclusive ischemia represents disproportionate mesenteric arteriolar vasospasm in response to severe physiologic stress such as shock; if untreated, early mucosal stress ulceration progresses to full-thickness injury. Mesenteric venous thrombosis arises from inherited or acquired hypercoagulable states (p.2587).
additionalDifferentials: Gastrointestinal malignancy (must be excluded in CMI before intervention)
Peptic ulcer disease and other causes of epigastric/postprandial pain
Inflammatory bowel disease (ischemic colitis is commonly confused with IBD)
Acute intestinal obstruction (especially strangulated obstruction with vascular insufficiency)
additionalInvestigations: CT angiography with thin (1-mm or finer) cuts, including venous phase for venous thrombosis (gold standard)
Fasting mesenteric duplex ultrasound (screening; SMA peak velocity)
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy (to exclude malignancy in CMI and assess colonic mucosa in ischemic colitis)
Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram (to identify embolic source such as atrial fibrillation; should not delay surgery)
Laboratory markers: leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis, lactic acidosis (support advanced ischemia but do not reliably distinguish reversible ischemia from necrosis)
Hypercoagulability workup in mesenteric venous thrombosis
redFlags: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings
Peritonitis and cardiovascular collapse (late findings indicating advanced ischemia)
Leukocytosis with metabolic/lactic acidosis suggesting advanced ischemia or necrosis
Black or green colonic mucosal discoloration on colonoscopy indicating full-thickness necrosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, or infective endocarditis in a patient with acute abdominal pain (embolic source)
harrison.prognosis: Acute mesenteric ischemia carries a mortality rate exceeding 50% and is among the most challenging diagnoses; the timeliness of diagnosis and treatment is the single most important determinant of survival. Chronic mesenteric ischemia managed with revascularization has favorable long-term outcomes, with endovascular stenting associated with about an 80% long-term success rate. Outcomes hinge on early recognition before progression to full-thickness bowel necrosis and peritonitis (p.2587-2588).
pitfalls: Anchoring on a benign cause and underestimating severity because abdominal pain is markedly out of proportion to a relatively unremarkable exam (p.2588).
Waiting for abnormal laboratory values before acting; lactate, leukocytosis, and acidosis may be normal early or fail to distinguish reversible ischemia from necrosis (p.2588-2589).
Performing mesenteric duplex without fasting, since bowel gas obscures flow and the postprandial vasodilation response (p.2587).
Mistaking ischemic colitis for inflammatory bowel disease (p.2589).
Overlooking nonocclusive ischemia in obtunded, critically ill patients in whom physical findings are obscured by the underlying illness (p.2589).

Failing to recognize that the proximal jejunum may be spared in SMA embolism while the rest of the small bowel to the transverse colon becomes ischemic, leading to incomplete bowel assessment (p.2589).
harrison.severityClassification: Ischemic colonic mucosal injury is graded by colonoscopy: mild = minimal mucosal erythema; moderate = pale mucosal ulcerations with extension into the muscular layer; severe = severe ulcerations with black or green mucosal discoloration consistent with full-thickness bowel-wall necrosis. Mechanically, mesenteric ischemia is classified as chronic (CMI) versus acute (AMI), and AMI is subclassified as arterio-occlusive (embolic or thrombotic), nonocclusive (vasospastic/hypoperfusion), or mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587, p.2589).
management: Emergency resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and systemic heparin anticoagulation for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia
Urgent revascularisation by surgical embolectomy, endovascular thrombectomy or stenting, or mesenteric bypass, to restore splanchnic flow
Laparotomy with resection of frankly necrotic bowel and a planned second-look procedure to reassess viability
Intra-arterial vasodilator such as papaverine and correction of the low-flow state, avoiding vasoconstrictors, in nonocclusive ischaemia
Anticoagulation as the mainstay for mesenteric venous thrombosis
Elective endovascular stenting or surgical bypass for chronic mesenteric ischaemia, with nutritional repletion of the malnourished patient
Cardiovascular risk factor modification, antiplatelet therapy and treatment of an embolic source such as atrial fibrillation
Vascular surgery-led multidisciplinary care with monitoring for recurrent ischaemia after revascularisation
